concepts_used: PESA Act 1996: Extension of Panchayati Raj to Scheduled Areas
Gram Sabha: Composition, Powers, and Constitutional Significance

solution.concept_anchor: PESA Gram Sabha powers vs. standard Part IX framework
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who correctly identify that PESA covers Fifth Schedule areas and gives Gram Sabhas primacy may mismatch the specific powers (A and C in particular) by confusing minor forest produce with land acquisition.
elimination_logic: Match A: Control over minor forest produce — this is a specific PESA Gram Sabha power. List II: this pairs with 3 (PESA Gram Sabha — mandatory primacy over natural resource management).
Match B: Powers and functions of Gram Sabha left to state legislature — this is standard Part IX (Article 243A). Pairs with 1 (standard Part IX framework — discretionary state grant).

Match C: Mandatory prior consultation before land acquisition — PESA provision. Pairs with 3... wait, A already takes 3. Reconsider: C pairs with 4 (PESA mandatory consultation provision for land acquisition).
Match D: OBC reservation in Panchayats — purely discretionary, state law. Pairs with 2 (state discretion, no constitutional mandate). Correct: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 = option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is conflating PESA's two distinct mandatory provisions — control over minor forest produce and prior consultation for land acquisition — by assigning both to a single List II entry. Students who know PESA gives Gram Sabhas strong powers may correctly identify A and C as PESA provisions but fail to distinguish their specific content, causing mismatches.
solution.final_explanation:
PESA 1996 creates a fundamentally different Gram Sabha framework compared to standard Part IX. Understanding which power belongs to which framework is the key distinction.

Correct matching: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2

• A (Minor forest produce control) — 3 (PESA Gram Sabha — mandatory natural resource primacy): PESA Section 4(m) gives Gram Sabhas ownership rights over minor forest produce in Fifth Schedule areas.
• B (Powers left to state legislature) — 1 (standard Part IX discretionary framework): Article 243A's enabling language — state legislature 'may' assign powers. The Gram Sabha has only what the state gives it.
• C (Land acquisition consultation) — 4 (PESA mandatory consultation before land acquisition/rehabilitation): PESA Section 4(i) requires prior consultation with Gram Sabhas and their recommendations before any land acquisition in scheduled areas.
• D (OBC reservation) — 2 (state discretion, no constitutional mandate): Article 243D does not mandate OBC reservation; states may provide for it but are not required to.

Value Addition:
• PESA also gives Gram Sabhas power to regulate money lending to tribals and manage village markets.
• Implementation gap: states are required to amend their Panchayat laws to conform to PESA — many have done so inadequately.
• The Forest Rights Act 2006 complements PESA by recognising Community Forest Rights at the Gram Sabha level.

concepts_used: Mandatory vs. Discretionary Provisions of Part IX
Three-Tier Structure under Article 243B

solution.concept_anchor: Mandatory provisions — three tiers, reservations, SEC elections

statement_analysis.statement: The constitution of Panchayats at all three tiers (village, intermediate, and district) is mandatory for every state, with no population-based exception.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 243B(2) allows states with a population below 20 lakh to not constitute an intermediate-level Panchayat — the three-tier mandate has a population-based exception.

statement_analysis.statement: The conduct of Panchayat elections through the State Election Commission is a mandatory provision that all states must comply with.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 243K mandates the establishment of an SEC and vests election conduct in it — this is a non-discretionary provision binding all states.

statement_analysis.statement: Reservations for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in Panchayats must be in proportion to their population in each Panchayat area and are mandatory across all states.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 243D(1) and (2) mandate proportional SC/ST reservations — this is binding on all states with no discretionary element.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who do not know the sub-20 lakh exception for the intermediate tier will mark Statement 1 as correct and choose (d) — all three correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 243B(2) contains an express exception for states below 20 lakh population regarding the intermediate tier. 'No population-based exception' is false. INCORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 2: Article 243K is mandatory — all states must have an SEC conducting Panchayat elections. CORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 243D mandates SC/ST proportional reservations in all states — no discretion. CORRECT.
Statements 2 and 3 correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 adds 'with no population-based exception' — a classic scope-extension that turns a generally true statement false. Most students know three tiers are 'mandatory' and miss the 20 lakh sub-clause. This tests whether students have read the precise constitutional text rather than relying on general descriptions.
solution.final_explanation:
Distinguishing mandatory from discretionary provisions, and knowing the precise conditions attached to mandatory provisions, is the critical skill for this topic.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The sub-20 lakh exception is carved into Article 243B itself — it is not a state discretion but a constitutional provision. States like Goa legitimately operate a two-tier system under this provision.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Every state must have an SEC (Article 243K) — this is non-negotiable. The ECI has no role; the SEC is the exclusive constitutional authority for Panchayat elections.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 243D(1) — seats reserved for SC in proportion to SC population; Article 243D(2) — seats reserved for ST in proportion to ST population. Both are mandatory with no discretionary element.

Value Addition:
• The mandatory provisions of Part IX: (i) three-tier structure (subject to 20 lakh exception), (ii) SC/ST/women reservations, (iii) five-year term, (iv) SEC-conducted elections, (v) SFC every five years.
• Discretionary provisions: devolution of 3Fs, OBC reservation, Gram Sabha powers.
• States that comply with all mandatory provisions but fail on devolution represent the implementation gap in Panchayati Raj.

solution.concept_anchor: CAG enabling role vs. social audit statutory mandate

statement_analysis.statement: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is constitutionally mandated under Part IX to audit the accounts of all Panchayati Raj institutions.
statement_analysis.reason: Part IX contains no mandatory provision for CAG audit of Panchayats — the CAG's role in auditing Panchayat accounts is enabling (through CAG's DPC Act) and depends on state government invitation or High Court direction.

statement_analysis.statement: Social audit of MGNREGA works at the Gram Panchayat level is mandated by the MGNREGA statute, not by Part IX of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 17 of MGNREGA mandates social audit by the Gram Panchayat — this is a statutory requirement under the MGNREGA Act, independent of Part IX.

statement_analysis.statement: The 73rd Amendment includes a provision requiring Gram Panchayats to publish their annual accounts and expenditure statements for public inspection.
statement_analysis.reason: Part IX contains no such provision for mandatory public disclosure of Panchayat accounts — this would be a statutory or regulatory requirement under state laws, not a constitutional mandate.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who believe CAG audit of Panchayats is constitutionally mandated (confusing it with CAG's broader constitutional mandate) will choose only Statement 1 as not correct, missing Statement 3.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: CAG audit of Panchayats is NOT mandated under Part IX — the constitutional text is silent. INCORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 2: MGNREGA Section 17 mandates social audit — this is correct; the statement is accurate and should NOT be chosen as 'not correct'.
Evaluate Statement 3: Part IX has no provision requiring annual account publication — this is a statutory/regulatory matter. INCORRECT.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a plausible-fabrication trap. A 'publication of accounts' requirement sounds like the kind of transparency provision that a modern constitutional amendment would include. But Part IX is focused on structure, elections, and reservations — detailed accountability provisions are left to statute. Students who reason from 'what ought to be' rather than 'what is' will mark Statement 3 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Panchayat accountability is governed by a patchwork of statutory and regulatory frameworks, not a comprehensive constitutional mandate. Part IX's silence on detailed audit and transparency is a design gap.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: CAG's audit of Panchayats is not constitutionally mandatory under Part IX. The 2nd ARC recommended making it mandatory, but this has not been enacted.
• Statement 2 — Correct: MGNREGA's social audit mandate (Section 17) is one of the strongest grassroots accountability mechanisms — conducted by state-level Social Audit Units, independent of the CAG.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Part IX has no provision mandating public disclosure of Panchayat accounts. States may require this under their Panchayati Raj Acts, but it is not a constitutional requirement.

Value Addition:
• The CAG audits Panchayat accounts only when the state government requests it or when High Courts direct it.
• Kerala, Karnataka, and Andhra Pradesh have relatively stronger Panchayat audit systems through their own state laws.
• The Ministry of Panchayati Raj's e-Gram Swaraj portal is an administrative transparency tool — not a constitutional mandate.

solution.concept_anchor: DPC location in Part IX-A not Part IX — covers both urban and rural
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who associate DPC with Panchayati Raj (73rd Amendment) will place it in Part IX rather than Part IX-A, choosing (a).
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The DPC is found in Article 243ZD — this article falls in Part IX-A (Municipalities), not Part IX. Placing it in Part IX is wrong.
Eliminate (b): DPC consolidates plans of BOTH Panchayats AND Municipalities — characterising it as an exclusively rural body misrepresents its constitutional mandate.
Eliminate (d): The Chairperson of DPC forwards the consolidated plan to the state government — the DPC is a planning body, not an approving authority that sends plans to the Governor.

Confirm (c): The four-fifths elected-member requirement from Panchayats and Municipalities (in proportion to rural-urban population) and the DPC's role as a planning (not executive) body are both accurately stated.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap: the DPC is taught in the context of Panchayati Raj, leading students to assume it is in Part IX. Its actual location in Part IX-A (Article 243ZD) reflects its dual rural-urban character. This is one of the most reliable 'Part IX vs. Part IX-A' confusion points in the topic.
solution.final_explanation:
The District Planning Committee bridges the institutional divide between Panchayats and Municipalities — which is why it sits in Part IX-A despite covering both.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Article 243ZD falls in Part IX-A (74th Amendment chapter on Municipalities), not Part IX.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: DPC consolidates plans of both Panchayats and Municipalities — the rural-only characterisation ignores the urban component.
• Option (c) — Correct: The four-fifths elected-member composition (proportional to rural-urban population) and DPC's nature as a planning (not executive) body are correctly stated.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Chairperson forwards the consolidated plan to the state government, not to the Governor directly.

Value Addition:
• The DPC concept emerged from the need for integrated district-level planning to avoid rural-urban planning silos.
• Metropolitan Planning Committees (Article 243ZE) perform a similar function for metropolitan areas.
• The DPC has no executive powers — it cannot direct Panchayats or Municipalities to implement specific projects.

solution.concept_anchor: 15th CFC basic and tied grants — Panchayat finance architecture

statement_analysis.statement: Under the 15th Central Finance Commission framework, grants to rural local bodies include both basic (untied) and tied components — tied grants being linked to specific outcomes like sanitation and drinking water.
statement_analysis.reason: The 15th CFC introduced a tied-untied grant architecture: basic grants are untied (Panchayats can use them for any purpose), while tied grants are linked to sanitation and drinking water supply — a significant design feature.

statement_analysis.statement: Central Finance Commission grants for Panchayats are transferred directly to Panchayat bank accounts, bypassing the state government entirely.
statement_analysis.reason: CFC grants flow to the state government first, which then transfers them to Panchayats — the state is the intermediary. Direct transfer to Panchayats is the reform direction but not the current constitutional mechanism.

statement_analysis.statement: Panchayats can impose taxes on property and water user charges only if the State Legislature has authorised them to do so under Article 243H.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 243H is enabling — Panchayats have no inherent taxing power. All tax and fee levying requires express state legislative authorisation.

statement_analysis.statement: Tied grants under the 15th CFC framework require Panchayats to spend funds exclusively on elementary education and primary health, reflecting the Eleventh Schedule priorities.
statement_analysis.reason: 15th CFC tied grants are specifically linked to sanitation (drinking water, open defecation free status) and drinking water supply — NOT elementary education or primary health.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who believe Statement 2 is correct (direct CFC-to-Panchayat transfer) and correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 will choose (b) instead of (a).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: 15th CFC tied grants linked to sanitation/drinking water — CORRECT.
Statement 2: Grants flow through state governments, not directly to Panchayats — INCORRECT.
Statement 3: Article 243H requires state authorisation for any tax/fee — CORRECT.
Statement 4: 15th CFC tied grants are for sanitation and water, not education/health — INCORRECT.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — 'Only two' = option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 uses 'Eleventh Schedule priorities' — a plausible connection since elementary education and primary health appear in the Eleventh Schedule. Students who reason from 'CFC supports devolution → CFC should support Eleventh Schedule subjects' will mark Statement 4 correct. In reality, the 15th CFC's tied grants focus narrowly on sanitation and drinking water — sector-specific, not Schedule-general.
solution.final_explanation:
Panchayat finance involves multiple sources and conditions — the 15th CFC's architecture is a specific, examinable design feature.

• Statement 1 — Correct: 15th CFC divided local body grants into basic (untied — 60%) and tied (40% for sanitation and drinking water) — this architecture gives Panchayats some spending discretion while linking a portion to outcome-based priorities.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The constitutional and administrative mechanism routes CFC grants via state governments. Direct benefit transfer to Panchayats has been proposed but not implemented constitutionally.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 243H's enabling language means Panchayats are fully dependent on state authorisation to raise any revenue. This is the root cause of Panchayat fiscal weakness.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: 15th CFC tied grants specifically target sanitation and drinking water — not education or health. The Eleventh Schedule subjects are for general devolution, not CFC grant categorisation.

Value Addition:
• 15th CFC allocated ₹2.36 lakh crore to local bodies (Panchayats + Municipalities) for 2021–26.
• Own-source revenue of Panchayats across India is estimated at less than 1% of local body expenditure.
• The tied-untied grant distinction was introduced to incentivise specific governance outcomes at the grassroots.

solution.concept_anchor: Two-child norm as Panchayat disqualification — Javed v. Haryana
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — A states that the Supreme Court upheld the two-child norm as a valid disqualification for Panchayat membership in Javed v. State of Haryana (2003). This is factually accurate. A is CORRECT.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — R states that Article 243F empowers state legislatures to prescribe disqualifications for Panchayat membership beyond those in the Constitution, and states are therefore free to add disqualifications by law. Article 243F does permit state law to prescribe additional disqualifications. R is CORRECT.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — R correctly identifies the legal basis (Article 243F) that allowed Haryana to enact the two-child norm. The Supreme Court's upholding of the norm was precisely because Article 243F permits states to legislate additional disqualifications. R does explain A causally — the legal source (Article 243F) is why the two-child norm is constitutionally valid.
Both A and R correct, R explains A — correct option is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is option (b) — students who know both facts are correct may reason that 'the Supreme Court upheld the norm on constitutional grounds, which is broader than just Article 243F — so R does not fully explain A'. This over-reads the causal requirement. R's identification of Article 243F as the enabling source is precisely the causal chain: state power under Article 243F → state law enacted two-child norm → Supreme Court upheld it as within Article 243F's scope.
solution.final_explanation:
The two-child norm as a Panchayat disqualification is a landmark intersection of constitutional law, reproductive rights, and local governance.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: In Javed v. State of Haryana (2003), the Supreme Court upheld the validity of Haryana's Panchayati Raj provision disqualifying persons with more than two children from contesting Panchayat elections.
• Reason (R) — Correct: Article 243F(1)(b) permits a state legislature to prescribe, by law, grounds of disqualification for membership. The Constitution sets a floor; states can add to it. This is the precise constitutional source of state authority to enact the two-child norm.
• Causal link — R explains A: The Supreme Court's rationale in Javed directly invoked states' power under Article 243F — the norm was upheld because it falls within the state's constitutional authority to legislate additional disqualifications.

Value Addition:
• The two-child norm has been enacted in several states — Rajasthan, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and Odisha among others.
• Critics argue it disproportionately affects marginalised communities with higher fertility rates.
• The Supreme Court distinguished Panchayat membership from fundamental rights — holding that the norm does not violate Articles 14 or 21.

solution.concept_anchor: Panchayat legislative power absence and Nyaya Panchayat constitutional silence

statement_analysis.statement: Panchayats exercise legislative powers over subjects in the Eleventh Schedule to the extent those subjects have been devolved by the state legislature.
statement_analysis.reason: Devolution of Eleventh Schedule subjects gives Panchayats executive/administrative authority, not legislative power. Panchayats cannot make laws; they implement functions delegated to them by state law.

statement_analysis.statement: The High Court of a state has jurisdiction to hear disputes arising from Panchayat elections through election petitions filed under the relevant state Panchayati Raj Act.
statement_analysis.reason: Election petitions from Panchayat elections go to the High Court — consistent with the constitutional design placing Panchayats entirely within the state domain; the Supreme Court has no original jurisdiction over Panchayat election disputes.

statement_analysis.statement: Nyaya Panchayats, despite having a historical existence in India, are not mentioned in Part IX of the Constitution and exist purely through state legislation.
statement_analysis.reason: Part IX is entirely silent on Nyaya Panchayats. Their existence depends on state-level statutory provisions — there is no constitutional basis in the 73rd Amendment for judicial functions at the grassroots.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who (incorrectly) believe Panchayats gain legislative powers over devolved subjects will mark Statement 1 as correct and choose (d).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Devolution means executive/administrative delegation — Panchayats cannot legislate. The Constitution is clear that law-making power remains with the state legislature. INCORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 2: High Courts hear Panchayat election petitions; the state judicial architecture governs this. CORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 3: Nyaya Panchayats are absent from Part IX — completely statutory. CORRECT.
Statements 2 and 3 correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 introduces the plausible-fabrication that 'devolution of legislative subjects = legislative powers for Panchayats'. This sounds logical — if Parliament devolves legislative subjects to Panchayats, surely they gain some legislative authority? But the constitutional text is unambiguous: Panchayats are executive bodies. The state legislature legislates; Panchayats implement.
solution.final_explanation:
Two fundamental limits on Panchayat authority — no legislative power, and no constitutional judicial function — frame this question.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Devolution of Eleventh Schedule subjects gives Panchayats administrative and executive functions — not the power to legislate. Panchayats can frame bye-laws only if state law specifically authorises bye-law making power — even this is a limited, delegated authority.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The High Court is the appropriate forum for Panchayat election disputes. Article 329 (parliamentary elections) has an analogue in state Panchayati Raj Acts that route election petitions to the High Court.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 73rd Amendment's silence on Nyaya Panchayats is deliberate — judicial organisation at the grassroots was left entirely to state governments. The Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008 is a separate and distinct development.

Value Addition:
• Panchayats may pass resolutions, adopt budgets, and issue notices — these are administrative acts, not legislation.
• Some states grant Gram Panchayats the power to make 'bye-laws' — these are subordinate legislation under state law, not independent legislative power.
• The Gram Sabha has no judicial function under Part IX — dispute resolution through traditional mechanisms is not constitutionally recognised in Part IX.

solution.concept_anchor: Sequence of major Panchayati Raj enactments post-73rd Amendment
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know PESA came after the 73rd Amendment but place the Gram Nyayalayas Act before the Forest Rights Act will choose (b) — reversing the two most recent events.
elimination_logic: 73rd Amendment effective date: April 24, 1993 — this is the starting anchor.
PESA 1996: Enacted in 1996 — directly after the 73rd Amendment to address Fifth Schedule area gap.
Forest Rights Act: Enacted in 2006 — the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act.

Gram Nyayalayas Act: Enacted in 2008 — establishing mobile grassroots courts. Correct order: 73rd Amendment (1993) → PESA (1996) → Forest Rights Act (2006) → Gram Nyayalayas Act (2008). This matches option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Forest Rights Act (2006) and Gram Nyayalayas Act (2008) are both post-73rd Amendment statutes related to grassroots governance. Students who know FRA and Gram Nyayalayas but are unsure of their years will reverse them. The 2-year gap (2006 vs. 2008) is the temporal precision being tested.
solution.final_explanation:
Post-73rd Amendment, a series of statutes progressively filled gaps in the grassroots governance framework. Sequencing them by enactment year is a standard UPSC format.

Correct sequence: 73rd Amendment (1993) → PESA 1996 → Forest Rights Act 2006 → Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008.

• 73rd Amendment (1992, effective 1993): The foundational legislation — constitutional status for Panchayati Raj.
• PESA 1996: Filled the Fifth Schedule area gap left by Article 243M — gave Gram Sabhas primacy in tribal areas.
• Forest Rights Act 2006: Recognised individual and community forest rights of scheduled tribes and traditional forest dwellers — complemented PESA's framework for tribal governance.
• Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008: Created mobile grassroots courts (Gram Nyayalayas) at the Panchayat level, staffed by First Class Judicial Magistrates — distinct from Nyaya Panchayats.

Value Addition:
• The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises Community Forest Rights (CFR) at the Gram Sabha level — a significant enhancement of Gram Sabha authority in forest governance.
• Gram Nyayalayas have jurisdiction over certain civil and criminal matters — they are not the same as traditional Nyaya Panchayats.
• MGNREGA (2005) also falls in this sequence and mandates Gram Panchayat as principal implementing authority.

solution.concept_anchor: SEC superintendence vs. State Legislature delimitation authority
elimination_logic: Identify the applicable rule: Under Article 243K, the SEC superintends, directs, and controls preparation of electoral rolls AND conduct of elections. However, delimitation of constituencies is NOT the SEC's function — it is determined by the State Legislature or a body authorised by it.
Apply to scenario: The SEC cannot delimit constituencies on its own — this power belongs to the State Legislature. The SEC's refusal to proceed is constitutionally justified.
Eliminate (a): The SEC does not have unilateral delimitation power — it cannot modify ward boundaries on its own authority.
Eliminate (b): The ECI has no jurisdiction over Panchayat elections — involving the ECI is constitutionally inappropriate.
Eliminate (d): The SEC cannot proceed with elections using old boundaries when new ward boundaries have been legally constituted — this would create legal invalidity. Select (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap: students confuse the SEC's broad 'superintendence, direction, and control' over elections with a power to delimit constituencies. The SEC controls the election process — but the constituency map is set by the State Legislature. This mirrors the ECI-Parliament relationship for Lok Sabha delimitation. Swapping these roles is the trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The SEC's powers are broad but precisely bounded. Understanding what falls within 'superintendence, direction, and control' versus what is reserved for the State Legislature is the key skill.

Applicable principle: Article 243K vests election management in the SEC but does not give it delimitation powers. Delimitation of Panchayat constituencies is determined by the State Legislature under Article 243K read with state Panchayati Raj Acts.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The SEC cannot unilaterally modify ward boundaries — this is a legislative function, not an electoral management function.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The ECI has absolutely no jurisdiction over Panchayat elections. Involving the ECI would be constitutionally inappropriate.
• Option (c) — Correct: The SEC is right to flag that delimitation is a legislative function. The State Legislature (or a body authorised by it) must delimit the new wards before the SEC can conduct elections under the new boundaries.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Conducting elections on superseded ward boundaries would be legally problematic — the SEC correctly withholds action pending proper delimitation.

Value Addition:
• The SEC can set the election schedule, prepare electoral rolls, and manage voting — but cannot draw constituency maps.
• High Courts can direct the State Legislature to complete delimitation — not the SEC to do it unilaterally.
• This SEC-vs-Legislature division mirrors the ECI-vs-Parliament division for Parliamentary elections under Article 324 read with the Delimitation Act.

solution.concept_anchor: 73rd and 74th Amendments — separate Acts, same effective date
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know the 73rd Amendment covers Articles 243–243O may confuse the exact upper boundary, thinking 243ZG is the endpoint of Part IX.
elimination_logic: Evaluate (a): Both Amendments were passed in 1992 — correct. But they came into force on April 24, 1993 — NOT in 1992. The effective year is wrong. INCORRECTLY matched.
Evaluate (b): 73rd Amendment = Part IX (Articles 243–243O); 74th Amendment = Part IX-A (Articles 243P–243ZG). This is precisely correct. CORRECTLY matched.
Evaluate (c): Eleventh Schedule has 29 subjects; Twelfth Schedule has 18 subjects. Swapping these (29 for urban, 18 for rural) is incorrect. INCORRECTLY matched.
Evaluate (d): Ward Committees are mandatory for municipalities with population above 3 lakh — not 1 lakh as stated. INCORRECTLY matched. Select (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is the temporal-swap trap: both amendments WERE enacted in 1992 but came into force in 1993. Students who recall '1992' as the associated year (which is the Act number year) may mark (a) as correct. The effective date — April 24, 1993 — is what matters for 'came into force'.
solution.final_explanation:
Comparative precision between the 73rd and 74th Amendments is a standard UPSC testing area. Article ranges, Schedule subjects, and operative dates are the key parameters.

• Option (a) — Incorrectly matched: Both amendments were enacted in 1992 but came into force on April 24, 1993 — the pair incorrectly states '1992' as the operative year.
• Option (b) — Correctly matched: Part IX (Articles 243–243O) governs rural Panchayati Raj; Part IX-A (Articles 243P–243ZG) governs urban Municipalities. This is the precise constitutional architecture.
• Option (c) — Incorrectly matched: The Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects) is the RURAL schedule under the 73rd Amendment; the Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects) is the URBAN schedule under the 74th Amendment — the pair reverses these.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: Ward Committees are mandatory for municipalities with population of 3 lakh or more (Article 243S), not 1 lakh.

Value Addition:
• April 24, 1993 — the common effective date — is observed as Panchayati Raj Diwas.
• Part IX spans Articles 243 through 243O (15 articles); Part IX-A spans Articles 243P through 243ZG.
• The Eleventh Schedule was inserted by the 73rd Amendment; the Twelfth Schedule by the 74th Amendment — both in 1993.
